nameStory: The "brown angle shades" gets its name from the distinctive angular, shadowy markings that create geometric patterns across its brown wings. These angled lines and shadows give the moth a camouflaged appearance that helps it blend perfectly with tree bark and fallen leaves.
description: The Brown Angle Shades is a medium-sized moth in the cutworm moth family, with wings that span about 1.5 to 2 inches across. Its wings display beautiful brown tones with intricate angular patterns and shadowy markings that create a mottled, bark-like appearance. Like other nocturnal moths, it's most active at night and often comes to outdoor lights during late summer and fall. This widespread species is found across northern North America, making it a familiar sight for moth enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for distinctive angular, zigzag lines and shadowy patches across brown wings that create a geometric camouflage pattern resembling tree bark

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized moth with wingspan of 42-50mm (about 1.5-2 inches) - larger than many common house moths but smaller than luna or cecropia moths

idTips.label: Wing Color
idTips.description: Rich brown tones ranging from chocolate to rusty brown, with subtle lighter and darker shades creating depth and texture

idTips.label: Resting Position
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings in a tent-like position over its body, pressed close to tree bark or wooden surfaces where it becomes nearly invisible

idTips.label: Body
idTips.description: Robust, fuzzy brown body that matches the wing coloration, with a slightly flattened appearance when pressed against surfaces

habitat: Brown Angle Shades moths are found in mixed woodlands, forest edges, and areas with diverse woody plants throughout New England. They're particularly common around alder swamps, coniferous forests with balsam fir, and areas where wild cranberry and plum grow. You'll often spot them near outdoor lights, on tree trunks, or resting on wooden structures like cabin walls and fence posts.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active during spring months. Look for overwintering pupae in soil or leaf litter if you're curious about their lifecycle.
seasonality.summer: Adults begin emerging in late July, becoming more common through August. This is when you'll start seeing them at porch lights and outdoor fixtures in the evening.
seasonality.fall: Peak activity occurs from September through October when adults are most abundant. They're actively seeking mates and laying eggs before winter arrives.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off after the first hard frosts. The species overwinters as pupae buried in soil or hidden in protected spots under logs and debris.

funFact: Despite being called "cutworm moths," the Brown Angle Shades caterpillars are actually beneficial garden visitors that only eat the leaves of woody plants like alder and fir trees, never touching your vegetables or flower beds!
confusionNotes: Brown Angle Shades can be confused with other brown nocturnal moths, but their distinctive angular wing markings set them apart from the more rounded or wavy patterns of most other species. Remember: "angles for Angle Shades" - if you see geometric, zigzag patterns rather than smooth curves or spots, you've likely found one.
contextualKnowledge: The family name "cutworm moths" comes from many species in this group whose caterpillars cut through plant stems at soil level, but this creates confusion since not all family members, including the Brown Angle Shades, actually exhibit this behavior.
compareHints: Brown Angle Shades is the only species in its genus Phlogophora found in New England, making it unique among our local moth fauna. Compared to other brown moths in the cutworm family, it's distinguished by its geometric angular markings rather than the kidney-shaped spots, smooth bands, or circular eyespots typical of related species. Its consistent brown coloration and sharp-angled patterns make it one of the more easily recognizable members of this large moth family.
